title: "How many ratings, and from whom: Reliability, rater differences, and the number of ratings needed in creativity ratings of football actions, a judge response theory analysis"

abstract: |
  Creative products are assessed by the consensus of independent raters, and how many raters are needed and how raters differ have been studied mostly with verbal and static material. Football actions are nonverbal behaviour produced under time pressure and observed in competition, and rating-design evidence for such products is lacking. In this exploratory study, 24 raters gave 9,046 ratings of 3,669 football actions on a 7-point creativity scale in an incomplete, connected design. We fitted a graded response model (GRM) and a judge response theory ladder from the rating-scale many-facet Rasch model to the generalized partial credit model, and examined reliability by the number of ratings per action, observed and simulated. The empirical reliability of the obtained scores was .689, against .969 for a hypothetical full panel; mean product-level reliability was .522 for actions with one rating and .699 with two. In this rater pool, the smallest number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 was four. Raters differed in severity, category use (share of lowest-category ratings .579 to .016), thresholds, discrimination and information; parameters of raters with about 50 ratings were imprecise. Likelihood-ratio tests rejected a shared category structure and equal discrimination (both *p* < .001), although the Bayesian information criterion favoured the constrained models in both cases. For such products, studies should report the reliability of the scores actually used, plan several ratings per action from domain-specific evidence, link raters through a common calibration set, and consider rater-adjusting scoring models, reporting their departure from raw means.

# Introduction

Creativity is widely regarded as a core competence. Employers rank creative thinking among the core skills of the workforce [@wef2025], the Programme for International Student Assessment assessed creative thinking in its 2022 cycle [@oecd2024], and in sport, creativity is considered a quality to be developed and evaluated in players [@safardilha2019; @santos2016]. [\[FILL IN: verify the framing claims attributed to wef2025, oecd2024, safardilha2019 and santos2016 against the PDFs (FI-17)\]]{.mark} Of the four facets of creativity, the person, the process, the product and the press [@batey2012], the product is the one that is judged by others, and each facet requires its own measurement approach [@barbot2019b]. Creative products are assessed by the consensus of independent raters who know the domain: the consensual assessment technique [CAT; @amabile1982; @hennessey2011; @kaufman2024]. In the CAT and judge response theory literature, raters are called judges; we use "raters" throughout. The consensus, however, is only as good as the panel that produces it.

## How many raters are enough is conditional

The reliability of CAT scores rests on aggregation. As @amabile1982 noted, by Spearman–Brown logic the reliability of a mean rating depends on the mean inter-rater correlation and on the number of raters, so that a larger panel compensates for lower agreement between individual raters. The reverse also holds: a high coefficient alpha from a large panel can mask low agreement between single raters. @kaufman2008a reported that 106 novices reached an alpha of .94 on poems while correlating .22 with experts. [\[FILL IN: verify the "mask" wording and the values .94 and .22 in kaufman2008a (FI-17)\]]{.mark} Moreover, consistency and absolute agreement are seldom distinguished in creativity research [@cseh2019; @stefanic2015].

How many raters are needed therefore depends on the reliability target, on the object of measurement (persons across tasks or single products), on rater expertise and training, on the scale and scoring format, on the heterogeneity of the products and on the domain. The published evidence bears this out, and each figure has to be read with its target and object. For student raters scoring short, homogeneous responses at the person level, D-studies projected that two trained raters for unusual uses and instances and three for consequences would reach a relative generalizability coefficient of at least .80 under average scoring [@silvia2008]; for caption writing, five graduate-student raters with 15 captions were projected to reach .80 for both relative and absolute coefficients [@kaufman2007]. For novices rating expert-domain products at the product level with Cronbach's alpha as the criterion, the picture is different: for poems, Kaufman et al.'s own Spearman–Brown projection to 10 novices gave .58 [@kaufman2008a]; for short stories, 100 random panels of 10 novices averaged .53 (range .35–.75) and for five engineering designs .66, against .93 and .86 for 10 experts, and 10-novice panels correlated .56 with experts on stories [@kaufman2013]. For open-ended products rated by non-experts, seven or more raters were needed for fashion outfits to exceed inter-rater and test-retest intraclass correlations of .70 consistently [@barth2021], and 10–15 undergraduates for creativity ratings of design products against a test-retest intraclass correlation of .70, with 15–20 for composite indices [@terai2026]. Where persons are measured across tasks and the person-by-task variance is large, adding raters stops helping: with two divergent-thinking items, no panel of one to 10 lay raters reached .80, and rater main effects, which indicate severity differences, accounted for 26.6% and 56.9% of the variance [@hass2018]; with two trained raters, five tasks were needed for a relative coefficient of .70 and more for absolute decisions [@vanhooijdonk2022]; and dependability was low for all rater groups on science tasks [@long2015]. Practice does not follow these figures closely. Most of 84 reviewed studies used fewer than 10 raters, about five on average [@long2022]; the common recommendation is five to 10 [@kaufman2008], and reported panels run from two to 134 raters [@cseh2019]. We located no study of the required number of raters for sport, for music as a headcount, for mathematics, for advertising or for programming. [\[FILL IN: verify the figures and verification levels of silvia2008, kaufman2007, kaufman2008a, kaufman2013, barth2021, terai2026, hass2018, vanhooijdonk2022, long2015, long2022, kaufman2008 and cseh2019 as used here (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

No general required number exists, then; the published figures are conditional on target, object, raters, scale and domain. @cseh2019 list the number of raters needed for a reliable consensus among the open questions of the CAT, and authors working with generalizability theory argue that each assessment procedure needs its own G- and D-study [@vanhooijdonk2022]. The evidence that does exist, moreover, comes from a narrow range of material.

## The verbal bias and the sport case

The rating-design evidence comes largely from verbal material, that is divergent-thinking responses, poems, stories, captions and metaphors, and from static products that raters inspect at leisure, such as collages, drawings and designs [@amabile1982; @kaufman2008a; @reiterpalmon2019; @saidmetwaly2017b; @paca2019; @acar2023; @acar2024]. Within sport, the standard tests are tests of generalist thinking expressed verbally or through drawing [@safardilha2019]. [\[FILL IN: check the wording and page of the safardilha2019 quotation and the characterisation of reiterpalmon2019, saidmetwaly2017b and paca2019 (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Football actions are a different kind of product. They are nonverbal behaviour produced under time pressure in a complex, dynamic environment: creative motor actions emerge from the interaction of performer and environment [@orth2017; @hristovski2011; @hristovski2012; @vaughan2019; @rasmussen2019], decisions in team sport are time-constrained option generation [@raab2007], and players have to process substantial information within a very short time [@memmert2011b]. Observed in competition, the product class has been argued to be more ecologically valid than laboratory and game-test settings [@safardilha2019; @memmert2011b; @joode2023; @cotter2019], and ratings of such actions exist [@kempe2018; @joode2023; @zahno2023; @zahno2024]. [\[FILL IN: verify the characterisation of orth2017, hristovski2011, hristovski2012 (author field), vaughan2019, rasmussen2019, raab2007, memmert2011b and cotter2019 (author field Cotter & Silvia) (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Sport creativity research, however, has concentrated on process measures, divergent thinking in game situations in particular [@memmert2007; @memmert2010; @memmert2013; @furley2015; @roca2018; @fink2018; @safardilha2019; @memmert2011b]. The few studies that had experts rate creative behaviour in football, in competition footage [@kempe2018], in games of academy players [@joode2023], in game-test situations [@memmert2010] or in verbal responses to video scenes [@roca2018], relied on three or four coaches or trained experts and reported the agreement of the panel, mostly as an intraclass correlation; averaging of the ratings and an intraclass correlation are reported for two of them [@roca2018; @joode2023], and the agreement index used by @kempe2018 is not named here; none examined how many raters are needed, how individual raters differ, or which scoring model suits the ratings. [\[FILL IN: verify kempe2018 (scale 0–10 or 1–10, reliability index, training, coaching licence), roca2018, memmert2010 and joode2023 (three or four raters, expertise, ICC, averaging), and the panel sizes of zahno2023 and zahno2024 (FI-17)\]]{.mark} Rating-design evidence for this product class is thus lacking, and answering these questions requires a method that treats the raters themselves as the object of study.

## From averages to judge response theory

Raw averages with alpha or Spearman–Brown treat raters as interchangeable and conflate panel size with agreement. Alpha ignores severity, which confounds raw means whenever different raters rate different products [@primi2019; @myszkowski2019]. Resampling raters from a large pool shows how reliability is distributed across panels of a given size, but the result is specific to that pool [@kaufman2013; @barth2021; @terai2026]. Generalizability theory decomposes the variance into rater, product and interaction components and projects relative and absolute coefficients to any number of raters in D-studies, but it still treats raters as interchangeable, needs near-balanced designs and cannot correct individual raters [@silvia2008; @hass2018; @vanhooijdonk2022]. Classical scoring remains the default in creativity measurement, and item response theory or generalizability theory are rarely used [@saidmetwaly2017b].

Many-facet Rasch models (MFRM) add rater severity as a facet, estimate and correct it in incomplete but connected designs, and flag misfitting raters [@linacre1989; @eckes2015]. @primi2019 showed that severity confounds scores when raters score different subsets of the products and that rater workload could be cut by about a third with severity-adjusted scores. Every Rasch-family model, however, assumes that all raters discriminate equally, and the rating-scale form assumes in addition that all raters share one category structure; differences in discrimination have no parameter and surface only as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021]. [\[FILL IN: verify primi2019 (workload cut by about a third) and eckes2015 as the source for the partial-credit MFRM (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Judge response theory (JRT) transposes item response theory to multiple-rater data: raters take the role of items, and their severity, category thresholds and discrimination are estimated individually under the graded response model or the generalized partial credit model. It yields scores with product-specific standard errors, reliability conditional on the creativity level, and an explicit model of rater behaviour in which part of the rater-by-product interaction becomes information rather than error [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]. It has since been applied to ratings of three-dimensional drawings [@barbot2023], to divergent-thinking ratings, for which a graded response model was retained [@pellegrino2025], to the planning of planned-missing rating designs [@forthmann2025; @goecke2024] and to rubric-coded responses to the PISA creative-thinking tasks [@myszkowski2025]. [\[FILL IN: verify pellegrino2025 (GRM retained), barbot2023 (model), forthmann2025 and goecke2024 (planned-missing designs) and myszkowski2025 (FI-17)\]]{.mark} We located no application to ratings of sport actions, apart from a Rasch analysis of a coach-completed questionnaire that rates players rather than actions [@shin2025]. Because the rating-scale and partial-credit models are constrained versions of the generalized partial credit model, the constraints become testable by model comparison instead of being imposed [@myszkowski2021]. Whether the flexibility of JRT is needed is therefore an empirical question.

## The present study

The present study analysed a large set of CAT-style creativity ratings of football actions given by 24 raters in a sparse but connected design, in which not every rater rated every action and most actions received few ratings. It was exploratory, and no confirmatory hypotheses were formulated. Three research questions were addressed.

- **RQ1 (number of ratings and reliability).** How reliable are the creativity scores obtained in this study, how does product-level reliability vary with the number of ratings an action received, and how many ratings per action are needed for reliable estimates in this rater pool, (a) as observed and (b) as simulated from the fitted model? How do these figures compare with a hypothetical full panel and with conventional agreement and consistency indices?
- **RQ2 (rater differences).** How do raters differ in severity, threshold location, scale use, discrimination and information, and how precisely are these differences estimated?
- **RQ3 (model constraints and consequences for scores).** (a) Are the Rasch-family constraints of a shared category structure and of equal discrimination tenable for these ratings? (b) How far do product scores and rankings depend on the scoring model, from the raw mean through the constrained models to the graded response model?

To answer these questions, we fitted a graded response model and a ladder of adjacent-category models by marginal maximum likelihood, estimated the reliability of the obtained scores overall and by number of ratings, projected reliability for one to 10 ratings per action and simulated the actual design topped up so that every action had at least four ratings, described the rater parameters with their uncertainty, and compared the graded response model scores with raw means and with the constrained models. Rater expertise and the design of the rating scale are not analysed.

# Method

## Overview

This was a CAT-style rating study in which raters independently rated the creativity of football actions, relative to one another and in a randomised order [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011]. The ratings were collected as part of a larger project. [\[FILL IN: context and purpose of the larger project (FI-1, FI-2)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: ethics approval (committee, reference number) and informed-consent procedure (FI-1)\]]{.mark} The analyses were exploratory. [\[FILL IN: preregistration status (FI-15)\]]{.mark}

## Raters

The raters came from two groups. The first group consisted of Bachelor's and Master's students who rated as part of their thesis projects. [\[FILL IN: confirm; recruitment and number of raters at the start of the first group (FI-1)\]]{.mark} The second group, raters R23 to R27, joined later. [\[FILL IN: background, recruitment and rating period of the second rater group (R23–R27), and how actions were allocated to them (FI-31)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: rater-pool description for both groups: football playing or coaching experience, any instruction or practice before rating, number of sessions per rater, demographics and compensation, or a statement that these were not recorded (FI-21)\]]{.mark} The final data comprised 24 raters, pseudonymised as R01 to R19 and R23 to R27; the gaps in the numbering arise because four raters were excluded (see Data preparation), and the numbers do not reflect the raters' workload. The raters gave between 46 and 1,174 ratings each (column "Ratings by rater" in the rater tables, e.g., @tbl-grm-rater-parameters).

## Products and stimulus material

Each rated product was a single football action; we use "product" for the analyses and "action" when referring to the football content. Actions were shown as video clips from recorded football matches and were identified with event data. [\[FILL IN: competitions and matches, action-selection rule, clip length, video source and number of matches (FI-2)\]]{.mark}

## Rating procedure

[\[FILL IN: rating software (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Raters were shown an instruction that defined creativity as the combination of originality and functionality of an action, functionality being its effectiveness in the game context (cf. the standard definition of creativity as originality and effectiveness by @runco2012). [\[FILL IN: verbatim instruction and creativity definition, original language and English translation (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Showing a definition departs to a minor degree from the CAT rule that raters receive no criteria [@hennessey2011] and resembles the procedure of trained-rater studies in sport [@kempe2018; @memmert2010]. Creativity was rated on a unipolar 7-point scale with verbal anchors at 1, 4 and 7. [\[FILL IN: verify the anchors and give their wording (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Raters could also mark a clip as "action not recognised". [\[FILL IN: exact wording of this option (FI-3)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: randomisation procedure, session length and breaks; no timing statements for R03, R06 and R13 (FI-3)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: data-collection period as a sentence (FI-32)\]]{.mark} Raters also rated technical correctness and aesthetic appeal, which are not analysed here. [\[FILL IN: wording and scales of these dimensions (FI-3)\]]{.mark}

## Rating design

[\[FILL IN: allocation of products to raters, including the second rater group: planned overlap, any common or benchmark set, randomisation, thesis-specific subsets or rater dropout; how products came to have 1, 2 or 3 or more ratings, including the latest collection; whether products with different numbers of ratings were rated by different raters or differ systematically (match, action type) (FI-4, FI-31)\]]{.mark} Not every rater rated every product, and most products received few ratings. The design was incomplete but connected: all raters and products formed a single connected component, so that all rater parameters and product scores lie on one scale [@eckes2015]. Marginal maximum likelihood estimation assumes that the missing ratings are ignorable given the design. The distribution of the number of ratings per product is shown in @fig-design-ratings-per-product in the supplement: 832 products received one rating, 2,107 two, 68 three, 153 four, 198 five, 137 six, 95 seven, 36 eight and 22 nine; 14 products received 10 ratings, 4 received 11, 2 received 12 and 1 received 13.

## Data preparation and final data

The raw export contained 10,447 rows. The 1,347 ratings marked "action not recognised" were removed; such ratings arise when video cutting, close-ups or other television artefacts leave the action not visible in the clip. [\[FILL IN: rate of "action not recognised" ratings by rater and, if available, by product (FI-22)\]]{.mark} One out-of-range value (0.0, given by R04) was removed. Twenty-one rater–product pairs had been entered more than once, one of them with conflicting values; the entry with the latest timestamp was kept, which removed 22 rows. This left 9,077 ratings by 28 raters.

Raters with fewer than 15 ratings were excluded because their up to seven rater-specific parameters cannot be estimated reliably: R20 (13 ratings), R21 (9), R22 (2) and R28 (7), together 31 ratings (@tbl-excluded-raters). [\[FILL IN: source or rationale for the exclusion criterion of 15 ratings (FI-23)\]]{.mark} One product rated only by these raters was dropped. Excluding them left the product scores nearly unchanged on average (*r* = .99994, mean absolute change 0.00204), with a largest change in one product score of 0.35026 (@tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion).

The final data are described in @tbl-design-summary: 9,046 ratings of 3,669 products by 24 raters, given on the scale 1–7 and coded 0–6 internally. Products received a mean of 2.466 ratings (median 2, range 1–13, harmonic mean 1.806), and 832 products received a single rating. The product-by-rater matrix had a fill of .103 and formed one connected component; 30 of the 276 rater pairs had no product in common, and the median overlap of rater pairs was 19 products. Eight raters never used at least one category (@tbl-category-usage; @fig-category-usage-shares): category 7 was never used by R01, R03, R06, R18, R25 and R26, categories 6 and 7 were never used by R17, and categories 5 and 7 were never used by R27, so that R27 has an unused category inside the observed range (an internal gap). Because thresholds are estimated only between categories a rater used, R17 and R27 have four thresholds, R01, R03, R06, R18, R25 and R26 five, and all other raters six. The thresholds of R27 separate other category boundaries than those of the other raters and are not directly comparable with them.

## Measurement models

Item response theory (IRT) models the probability of each response as a function of a latent attribute and of item parameters [@lord1980; @embretson2013; @ayala2022]. Rasch models constrain all items to discriminate equally, which makes the raw score a sufficient statistic [@rasch1960; @bond2020]. Their polytomous forms, the rating scale model [RSM; @andrich1978] and the partial credit model [PCM; @masters1982], differ in whether all items share one category structure; the generalized partial credit model [GPCM; @muraki1992] and the graded response model [GRM; @samejima1969] add item-specific discrimination. The GPCM and its Rasch-family special cases model the odds of adjacent categories, whereas the GRM models the cumulative probability of a response above each category.

All models here share the JRT frame [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]: raters take the role of items, products the role of persons, and product creativity is a single latent dimension $\theta$ with a normal distribution and a mean of 0. Its variance was fixed at 1 in M3 and the GRM and estimated in M1 and M2, whose discriminations are fixed. A rater's threshold $b_k$ is the $\theta$ at which a rating above category $k$ becomes more likely than a rating of $k$ or below. The discrimination $a$ expresses how sharply a rater's ratings separate products of different creativity. In the GRM, thresholds are expressed relative to discrimination, so threshold spacing is partly the same fact as discrimination.

The adjacent-category ladder comprised three nested models, each with raters as items. M1 (rating-scale MFRM) was the rating scale model with a rater severity parameter, which corresponds to a two-facet many-facet Rasch model with a shared rating scale when products and raters are the facets [@linacre1989; @eckes2015; @primi2019]; it was estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with a normal product distribution in `sirt::rm.facets` [@robitzsch2025]. M1 is the only model in the ladder in which all raters share one category structure. M2 (partial-credit MFRM) was the partial credit model with rater-specific thresholds, which corresponds to a many-facet Rasch model with a rater-specific category structure [@eckes2015]; like every Rasch model, it assumes equal discrimination. M3 (GPCM) was the generalized partial credit model, which additionally gives each rater their own discrimination. M2 and M3 were estimated with the R package mirt [@chalmers2012].

The retained scoring model was a GRM with rater-specific discriminations and thresholds, estimated in mirt; its thresholds are ordered by construction. It was estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with the expectation–maximisation (EM) algorithm (61 quadrature points, tolerance 0.0001), with standard errors from Oakes' identity [@chalmers2018]. The model converged after 436 iterations with a positive definite information matrix (@tbl-grm-convergence).

## Model comparison

Two likelihood-ratio (LR) tests were computed within the ladder: M1 (rating-scale MFRM) against M2 (partial-credit MFRM) for a shared against a rater-specific category structure, and M2 against M3 (GPCM) for equal against rater-specific discriminations. For all four models, the log-likelihood, the Akaike information criterion (AIC), the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) and the sample-size adjusted BIC (SABIC) were computed, with the difference to the best model on each criterion. The GRM, which is not nested in the ladder, was compared by information criteria only. Three caveats apply. The M1–M2 test compares models estimated in different software (sirt and mirt), so it is approximate. Its degrees of freedom (105) lie below the formula value $(J-1)(K-2) = 115$ for $J$ raters and $K$ categories, because the observed degrees of freedom are smaller by the number of categories raters never used, that is, unused end categories and any internal gap (@tbl-category-usage); the internal gap of R27 also makes the nesting of M1 in M2 approximate. Finally, no model without rater effects was fitted, so severity differences were not tested on their own.

## Model adequacy

Infit and outfit mean squares [@wright1982] were computed for each rater under M1 and the GRM. Their expected value is 1. Values outside 0.7–1.3 are flagged in the rater overview (@tbl-rater-overview); with about two ratings per product, values below 1 are expected, because each product's score is estimated from the very ratings being checked, so flags below 0.7 are read as a property of the design rather than as misfit, and no further cut-offs were applied. The S-X² statistic [@orlando2000; @kang2008] requires complete data, so the missing ratings were imputed 20 times from the fitted model and the statistic was averaged. About 90% of the cells were imputed, so the test is conservative. Local dependence was examined with Yen's Q3 [@yen1984], the correlation of two raters' residuals over the products both rated. Q3 was computed for rater pairs with at least three jointly rated products and residual variance in both raters (222 of 276 pairs). Because Q3 is negatively biased when few raters rate each product [@christensen2017], pairs were compared by their deviation from the mean Q3 over all computable pairs. A pair was flagged when it had at least 30 jointly rated products and deviated from this mean by more than 0.2. This criterion has no reference distribution. The global statistic C2 [@cai2014] could not be computed, because it needs the joint distribution of every rater pair and 30 of 276 pairs share no products.

## Scores, reliability and the two simulations

Product scores were expected a posteriori (EAP) estimates $\hat\theta$ with the posterior standard deviation (PSD) as their standard error. The primary index was the empirical marginal reliability of the scores actually obtained, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) / [\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) + \overline{\mathrm{PSD}^2}]$. For comparison, the model-based marginal reliability [@green1984], which refers to a hypothetical product rated by all raters, was computed with mirt and checked on a $\theta$ grid. Ninety-five percent intervals for both came from 200 accepted draws of the parameters from their asymptotic normal distribution (estimates and Oakes covariance matrix); for the empirical reliability, products were also resampled. A draw that did not define a valid GRM (some $a \leq 0$ or thresholds out of order) was rejected and replaced; 43 draws were rejected. The intervals are therefore conditional on valid parameter sets and approximate, especially for raters with few ratings.

At the product level, rel~post~ $= 1 - \mathrm{PSD}^2$ was computed. Because it is defined relative to the unit prior variance of $\theta$, it partly reflects the prior when a product has one or two ratings. As a check, rel~info~ $= I/(I+1)$ was computed from the information $I$ of the product's own raters at $\hat\theta$. Both were summarised by the number of ratings each product received (column "Ratings per product" in @tbl-grm-reliability-by-n).

Conventional reliability indices assume a complete design or must be adapted to an incomplete one [@hove2024], so we report them only as reference values for common practice. Cronbach's alpha [@cronbach1951] was computed from pairwise covariances over all usable raters and on the largest fully crossed block of raters and products [\[FILL IN: why six raters (R26, R19, R14, R02, R12, R27) were not usable for the pairwise alpha; which three raters form the crossed block (FI-9)\]]{.mark}, and Krippendorff's ordinal alpha [@hayes2007] measured the agreement of single ratings. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals came from bootstrapping products (1,000 replications). For the pairwise alpha, 647 of the 1,000 replications could be computed; in the other 353, some rater pair lost all shared products. The interval rests on the computable replications and is approximate and possibly biased.

Two simulations from the fitted GRM addressed the number of ratings needed (RQ1b). The criterion was a reliability of .80, the value used as the target in the generalizability studies cited above [@silvia2008; @kaufman2007; @hass2018], where it is a person-level generalizability or phi target; here it is applied to the empirical marginal reliability of product scores. In the projection, products with $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$ were simulated; each received $k$ ratings ($k$ = 1 to 10) from $k$ distinct raters of the panel drawn at random, each rater being equally likely to be drawn, so that the draws do not reproduce the raters' actual workloads in the study. Ratings were generated from the fitted GRM and scored with its parameters, which were treated as known. The projection used 50 replications of 2,000 simulated products per $k$ (seed 20260713) and gave the empirical marginal reliability (mean and 95% range over replications) and the mean rel~post~ for each $k$; the smallest $k$ at which the simulated empirical reliability reached .80 is reported. The top-up simulation was built on the actual design: it kept the actual assignment of raters to products, that is, which raters had rated which product, but not the ratings themselves. Two designs were simulated with the same machinery. In the actual design, each product kept exactly the raters who had rated it. In the design with at least four ratings per product, each product kept its raters, and every product with fewer than four ratings was assigned additional raters, drawn at random with equal probability and without replacement from the panel raters who had not rated it, until it had four; products with four or more ratings were unchanged. In each of 50 replications, every real product received a creativity value $\theta$ drawn from $N(0, 1)$, all ratings in the design, for the kept and the added rater–product pairs alike, were generated from the fitted GRM, and the products were scored by EAP with the parameters treated as known. The real ratings were not reused; the actual-design row is a validation of the simulation, which should reproduce the observed empirical reliability of the real scores. In both simulations the ranges reflect simulation variability only, not parameter uncertainty, and the observed data remain primary. Observed and simulated values are shown side by side in @fig-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated and @tbl-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated; they are different quantities, the observed mean rel~post~ of the actual products and the simulated empirical marginal reliability.

## Rater parameters, severity, information and response styles

Rater severity under M1 was reported with its standard error (0 = average rater, higher = stricter; @fig-m1-rater-severity, with the values in @tbl-rater-overview). The GRM discrimination $a$ and thresholds $b_k$ of each rater were reported with their standard errors (@tbl-grm-rater-parameters; @fig-grm-rater-discrimination-ci shows $a$ with ±1.96 *SE*). Rater information integrated over the standard normal distribution of $\theta$ is called the rater's average information; each rater's share of the full-panel information was computed overall and at selected values of $\theta$, with 95% intervals from the same parameter draws as above (@tbl-grm-rater-information-ci; @tbl-grm-information-summary). Descriptive response styles on the raw 1–7 scale (@tbl-overview-rater-response-styles) comprised each rater's mean, median, standard deviation, interquartile range, number of categories used, entropy (natural logarithm), and the shares of ratings in the lowest category (1), the highest category (7), the extreme categories (1, 7) and the middle categories (3–5); they are not adjusted for which products each rater saw and carry no per-rater uncertainty. @tbl-rater-overview collects, per rater, the number of ratings, the raw mean, the severity (M1), the discrimination $a$ (GRM), the share of the panel information with its interval, the GRM infit and outfit with flags, and the categories never used.

## Score agreement and sensitivity

Each product's raw mean rating, the common-practice score that treats raters as interchangeable, was compared with its GRM score separately for products with one, two, and three or more ratings. Because the raw mean takes few distinct values (with one rating, only seven), agreement was described by Kendall's $\tau_b$, by the share of product pairs with different raw means that the GRM score orders the other way round (pairs in reversed order), and by the mean and maximum range of GRM scores among products with the same raw mean. To describe the dependence on the choice among the four models, the EAP scores of all models were correlated (Pearson and Spearman); relative to the GRM, the absolute shift in percentile rank (0–1 scale) and the share of products changing quintile were computed. M1 was also re-estimated with the default integration grid of sirt as a check. Finally, the GRM was refitted with all 28 raters.

## Software and availability

All models were estimated in R with mirt [@chalmers2012] and sirt [@robitzsch2025]; psych and an R package for Krippendorff's alpha were used for the conventional indices, and Python for display. [\[FILL IN: versions of R, mirt, sirt and psych, and the name and version of the package used for Krippendorff's alpha (FI-6)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: data and code availability statement; only pseudonymised rater IDs are shared (FI-15)\]]{.mark}

# Results

The results follow the three research questions: the reliability of the scores and the number of ratings (RQ1), the differences between raters (RQ2), and the tenability of the model constraints and their consequences for the scores (RQ3). All analyses used the final data in @tbl-design-summary; the degree distributions of the design are shown in @fig-overview-degree-distributions in the supplement. We first report the scoring model.

## Scoring model

As shown in @tbl-model-fit, the GRM had the lowest AIC (27,258.550) and SABIC (27,737.316) of the four models, whereas BIC was lowest for M1 (rating-scale MFRM; 28,235.202), with the GRM 4.161 above it (28,239.363). The GRM and M3 (GPCM) have the same number of parameters (158), so their comparison reduces to the log-likelihood (−13,471.275 vs. −13,495.966), and the GRM is lower by 49.381 on AIC, BIC and SABIC alike. The GRM converged after 436 EM iterations with a positive definite information matrix (@tbl-grm-convergence). No rater's S-X² was significant (*p* from .328 to .665; @tbl-grm-rater-fit). Under the GRM, infit ranged from 0.429 (R02) to 0.980 (R18) and outfit from 0.402 (R02) to 0.971 (R18), all below 1; 15 raters were flagged in @tbl-rater-overview, all for values below 0.7 and none for values above 1.3. The mean Q3 over the 222 computable pairs was −.202, and 28 pairs were flagged; of the 10 shown in @tbl-grm-q3-flagged, eight deviated negatively and two (R09–R23 and R10–R11) positively. C2 could not be computed (see Model adequacy).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-model-fit >}}

## Reliability of the scores and number of ratings (RQ1)

@tbl-reliability-overview sets the reliability of the obtained scores against the other indices and states what each refers to. The empirical marginal reliability of the obtained scores was .689 [.669, .703]. The model-based marginal reliability for a hypothetical product rated by all raters was .969 [.965, .974], with a grid check of .969 (@tbl-grm-reliability-ci; @fig-grm-panel-information). Cronbach's alpha from pairwise covariances, which refers to the consistency of the unweighted rater mean, was .949 [.926, .958] (18 raters, 1,946 products); its interval is approximate, because it rests on the 647 of 1,000 bootstrap replications that could be computed (@tbl-naive-indices). On the fully crossed block, Cronbach's alpha was .750 [.684, .800] (3 raters, 261 products). Krippendorff's ordinal alpha, which refers to the agreement of single ratings, was .391 [.363, .417] (24 raters, 2,837 products).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-reliability-overview >}}

@tbl-grm-reliability-by-n summarises the observed product-level reliability by the number of ratings each product received. Mean rel~post~ was .522 for the 832 products with one rating, .699 for the 2,107 with two and .756 for the 68 with three; it rose overall with the number of ratings, to .948 at 12, with two exceptions: .897 at 10 ratings after .915 at nine, and .947 at 13 after .948 at 12. Mean PSD fell from 0.684 to 0.228, with the same exceptions at 10 (0.314) and 13 (0.230). The rows from 10 ratings upward rest on 14, 4, 2 and 1 products. No mean reached the full-panel value of .969. Products with the same number of ratings differed in rel~post~ (@fig-grm-rel-post-by-n). These values are observed: products did not receive their number of ratings through a design manipulation (see Rating design). [\[FILL IN: how products came to have their number of ratings (FI-4)\]]{.mark}

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-reliability-by-n >}}

@fig-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated places the observed means next to the simulated reliability of the projection; the values are given in @tbl-grm-reliability-projection and @tbl-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated in the supplement (see also @fig-grm-reliability-projection). The simulated empirical reliability rose at every step, from .530 [.513, .544] at one rating to .705 [.696, .713] at two, .787 [.778, .797] at three, .834 [.827, .841] at four and .928 [.925, .931] at 10; the smallest number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 was four. The observed means lay inside the simulated 95% range at one, two and eight ratings and below it at three to seven, nine and 10 ratings. The two quantities are not the same: the observed values are mean rel~post~ of the actual products, the simulated values the empirical marginal reliability of simulated products.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated >}}

@tbl-grm-reliability-min-ratings gives the top-up simulation. The simulated actual design, in which each product kept the raters who had rated it, gave an empirical reliability of .686 [.675, .695] (mean rel~post~ .687), against the observed .689 of the real scores. The design in which every product had at least four ratings, with simulated ratings for 6,778 added rater–product pairs in 3,007 products (15,824 simulated ratings in total), gave .835 [.829, .840].

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-reliability-min-ratings >}}

Across all products, rel~post~ had a median of .712 and an interquartile range of .191 (first and third quartiles .599 and .789), with values from .068 to .954 (@tbl-grm-reliability-summary; @fig-grm-rel-post-histogram); its relation to $\hat\theta$ is shown in @fig-grm-rel-post-by-theta. rel~post~ and rel~info~ correlated at *r* = .947, and 229 products differed by more than .1 (@fig-grm-rel-consistency).

## Rater differences (RQ2)

@fig-category-usage-shares shows how each rater used the seven categories; the response-style values are given in @tbl-overview-rater-response-styles and @fig-overview-rater-response-styles in the supplement. Rater means ranged from 1.760 (R06) to 3.836 (R18) and standard deviations from 1.022 (R01) to 1.953 (R19). The share of ratings in the lowest category (1) ranged from .579 (R06) to .016 (R13). The share in the highest category (7) was highest for R19 (.080), and eight raters (R01, R03, R06, R17, R18, R25, R26 and R27) gave no rating of 7; R27 also never used category 5. The share in the middle categories (3–5) was highest for R13 (.799), followed by R18 (.764) and R12 (.735), and lowest for R06 (.192). Entropy ranged from 1.191 (R06) to 1.903 (R09; mean rating 3.643). Across all ratings, category 1 received 2,179 ratings and category 2 received 2,355, whereas category 7 was the rarest, with 128 (@fig-overview-rating-distribution). These response-style values are descriptive and have no per-rater uncertainty.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-category-usage-shares >}}

@tbl-rater-overview collects the rater-level results, and @fig-m1-rater-severity shows the severity of each rater under M1 (rating-scale MFRM) with its 95% interval next to the rater's raw mean. Severity ranged from −0.878 (*SE* 0.066, R24) to 1.369 (*SE* 0.057, R06), a span of 2.247 logits; 13 raters lay below and 11 above the average rater. The order of the severities did not follow the order of the raw means exactly: R18 had the highest mean rating (3.84) but the second-lowest severity (−0.79).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-rater-overview >}}

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-m1-rater-severity >}}

@tbl-grm-rater-parameters gives the GRM parameters with their standard errors; the category response functions are shown in @fig-grm-category-response-functions. Over all 24 raters, the first threshold $b_1$ ranged from −6.25 (R18, 55 ratings, *SE* 2.86) to 0.25 (R06, *SE* 0.05); the next lowest was −3.36 (R13, *SE* 0.47), and R06 was the only rater with a positive $b_1$. Threshold spacing also differed, for example from −0.67 ($b_1$) to 1.99 ($b_6$) for R02 and from −3.36 to 4.31 for R13; in the GRM, spacing is partly the same fact as discrimination. R17 and R27 had four thresholds, R01, R03, R06, R18, R25 and R26 had five, and all other raters had six; because of its internal gap, the thresholds of R27 are not compared with those of the other raters.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-rater-parameters >}}

Discrimination is shown with its intervals in @fig-grm-rater-discrimination-ci. It ranged from 0.66 (R18, 55 ratings, *SE* 0.27) to 3.19 (R26, 46 ratings, *SE* 1.72). The next highest values came from raters with many ratings as well as few: R06 3.10 (520 ratings, *SE* 0.45), R27 3.04 (47, *SE* 0.91), R25 3.01 (138, *SE* 0.47) and R24 2.89 (190, *SE* 0.37); the next lowest was R09 at 0.93 (400 ratings, *SE* 0.15). R16 had 2.47 (268, *SE* 0.26), R01 1.82 (*SE* 0.13), R02 2.71 (*SE* 0.35) and R23 1.75 (*SE* 0.13). The largest standard errors of $a$ belonged to R26 (1.72), R19 (1.01) and R27 (0.91).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-grm-rater-discrimination-ci >}}

Average information and information shares are given with 95% intervals, based on the same 200 accepted parameter draws, in @tbl-grm-rater-information-ci and @fig-grm-rater-information-ci. Average information ranged from 0.13 [0.02, 0.39] (R18) to 2.52 [0.11, 6.75] (R26), and shares from .004 [.000, .011] (R18) to .074 [.003, .178] (R26). Raters with many ratings had, for example, 0.28 [0.13, 0.48] (R09), 0.86 [0.66, 1.05] (R01) and 1.96 [1.11, 2.97] (R02). The widest intervals belonged to R26, R19 (2.03 [0.27, 5.31]) and R27 (2.01 [0.50, 4.12]). Raters provided information in different regions of the latent scale (@fig-grm-rater-information; @tbl-grm-information-summary). The location of maximum information was highest for R01 (2.800), R16 (2.400) and R06 (2.300) and lowest for R13 (−0.600). Shares varied with $\theta$ (@fig-grm-information-shares): R06 contributed .001 of the panel information at $\theta = -2$ and .082 at $\theta = 2$, whereas the largest shares at $\theta = -2$ came from R12 (.137) and R24 (.120). All intervals in this section are conditional on valid parameter draws.

## Model constraints and consequences for the scores (RQ3)

The LR test of M1 (rating-scale MFRM) against M2 (partial-credit MFRM), which concerns the shared category structure of M1, gave $\chi^2(105) = 840.447$, *p* < .001 (@tbl-lr-tests); AIC favoured M2 (27,418.524 vs. 28,048.971), whereas BIC favoured M1 (28,235.202 vs. 28,256.560). The test of M2 against M3 (GPCM), which concerns equal discrimination, gave $\chi^2(23) = 156.593$, *p* < .001; AIC favoured M3 (27,307.931 vs. 27,418.524), whereas BIC favoured M2 (28,256.560 vs. 28,288.744). Both constraints were thus rejected by the LR test and AIC but not by BIC.

Within the ladder, the M3 discriminations ranged from 0.305 (R18, *SE* 0.141) to 2.221 (R27, *SE* 0.873), with a median of 1.240, a ratio of the largest to the smallest of 7.277 and a standard deviation of 0.550 (@tbl-discrimination-m3; @tbl-discrimination-summary). Nine raters had unordered step parameters under M2 and eight under M3 (@tbl-threshold-order). Under M1, R09 (infit 1.083, outfit 1.060), R17 (1.323, 1.167) and R18 (1.170, 1.231) had values above 1, and R12 had the lowest (0.260, 0.278; @tbl-rater-fit-m1).

@tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm and @fig-raw-mean-vs-theta compare each product's raw mean rating with its GRM score within groups of products with the same number of ratings. For the 832 products with one rating, Kendall's $\tau_b$ was .833, and .041 of the pairs with different raw means were in reversed order. Products with the same single rating received GRM scores that spanned on average 1.229 and at most 1.430; in the one-rating panel of @fig-raw-mean-vs-theta, this appears as vertical spread at each rating (points are jittered horizontally). For the 2,107 products with two ratings, $\tau_b$ was .818, .066 of the pairs were in reversed order, and the range of GRM scores at equal raw mean was 1.531 on average and 2.170 at most. For the 730 products with three or more ratings, the values were .849, .071, 0.537 and 1.317. The range at equal raw mean reflects differences in both the threshold location and the discrimination of the raters who gave the ratings and, with two or more ratings, the combinations of ratings behind the same mean.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm >}}

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-raw-mean-vs-theta >}}

@tbl-score-agreement compares the scores of the constrained models with the GRM scores. Relative to the GRM, M1 (rating-scale MFRM) scores correlated at .977 (Pearson) and .979 (Spearman), and .206 of products changed quintile, with a mean percentile shift of .042. For M2 (partial-credit MFRM), the correlations were .985 and .984, and .155 of products changed quintile, with a mean percentile shift of .032; for M3 (GPCM), they were .996 and .996, and .081 changed quintile, with a mean percentile shift of .016. Among the ladder models, Pearson correlations ranged from .981 to .993 and Spearman correlations from .984 to .996 (@tbl-theta-correlations); M1 re-estimated with the default integration grid correlated at 1.000 with M1.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-score-agreement >}}

No confidence intervals are available for these agreement statistics. The contrast between M1 and the GRM combines the rater constraints with a change of link function. All comparisons show that the scores differ, not which score is more accurate.

## Sensitivity to the rater exclusion

Refitting the GRM with all 28 raters (9,077 ratings, 3,670 products) changed the empirical marginal reliability from .68896 to .68837 and the model-based marginal reliability from .96893 to .97142 (@tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion). Over the 3,669 common products, the scores of the two fits correlated at .99994 (Pearson); the mean absolute difference was 0.00204, the maximum 0.35026, and .00273 of products changed quintile. Over the 24 common raters, discriminations correlated at .99802, with a maximum absolute difference of 0.19349.

# Discussion

This study described the reliability of creativity scores for football actions as a function of the number of ratings, the differences between raters, and the dependence of the scores on the scoring model. The reliability of the obtained scores was well below that of a hypothetical full panel; one or two ratings per action gave limited precision, and in this rater pool the smallest number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 was four. Raters differed in severity, scale use, discrimination and information, with imprecise estimates for raters with about 50 ratings. The shared category structure of M1 (rating-scale MFRM) and equal discrimination, which all Rasch-family models assume, were rejected by the LR test and AIC but not by BIC. Raw means and model-based scores ordered actions partly differently. These results rest on the GRM, which had the lowest AIC and SABIC, whereas BIC favoured M1 by 4.161.

## RQ1: Reliability and the number of ratings per action

The conventional figures refer to the reliability of the mean over a large or complete panel: the full-panel reliability was .969 and the pairwise Cronbach's alpha .949. The scores actually obtained had an empirical reliability of .689 [.669, .703], and this is the figure that matters when the scores are used. The difference follows the Spearman–Brown logic described by @amabile1982: the panel coefficients refer to more ratings per product than the products received. The contrast between Krippendorff's alpha for single ratings (.391) and the pairwise Cronbach's alpha (.949) illustrates the point of @kaufman2008a that a high alpha can coexist with low agreement between individual raters, and the distinction between consistency and absolute agreement that is seldom drawn in creativity research [@stefanic2015; @cseh2019]. [\[FILL IN: verify the kaufman2008a, stefanic2015 and cseh2019 attributions (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

Actions with one rating had a mean product-level reliability of .522, and actions with two ratings .699. Where individual action scores are used, for example to select creative actions, one or two ratings per action gave limited precision in these data. Reliability rose overall with the number of ratings, but the rows at 10 and 13 ratings, which fall below the preceding rows, rest on 14 and 1 products, and the by-n values are observational: how an action came to have its number of ratings was not manipulated. Precision also differed among products with the same number of ratings and with their location on $\theta$ (@fig-grm-rel-post-by-n; @fig-grm-rel-post-by-theta), and for one or two ratings, rel~post~ partly reflects the prior.

The two simulations give a figure for the number of ratings needed in this rater pool. In the projection, the smallest number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 was four (.834), and the actual design topped up so that every action had at least four ratings gave .835, the dashed line for the topped-up design in @fig-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated. Under the stated assumptions, that raters are drawn at random with equal probability, that the parameters are known and that all ratings, including those of the actual rater–product pairs in the top-up simulation, follow the fitted GRM, these values describe this rater pool and this scale, not a general requirement. The observed means at three to seven, nine and 10 ratings lay below the simulated range. Several readings are possible: the two quantities differ, the products with several ratings were rated by particular raters rather than by random draws from the panel, and some of the rows are small. [\[FILL IN: whether products with different numbers of ratings were rated by different raters (FI-4)\]]{.mark} The data do not decide between these readings.

Read against the cross-domain evidence, with the reliability target and the object of measurement stated, four ratings for .80 in these product-level ratings by this rater pool can be set beside the two or three trained raters projected for short divergent-thinking responses, measured at the person level against a relative generalizability coefficient of .80 [@silvia2008], the finding that 10 lay raters did not reach an adequate Cronbach's alpha for expert-domain products, where 10 experts did [@kaufman2008a; @kaufman2013], and the 7 to 15 non-experts needed for fashion and design products against inter-rater and test-retest intraclass correlations of .70 [@barth2021; @terai2026]. The expert panels of the sport studies comprised three or four raters, rating competition footage [@kempe2018], game play of academy players [@joode2023], game-test situations [@memmert2010] or verbal responses to video scenes [@roca2018], and reported the agreement of the panel, mostly as an intraclass correlation and in two cases of averaged ratings [@roca2018; @joode2023], rather than the number of ratings needed for a target reliability; whether coaches need fewer ratings than this rater pool is untested here, because rater expertise was not analysed.

## RQ2: Raters differ

Severity under M1 spanned 2.247 logits, from R24 to R06. This span is larger than the ranges @primi2019 report for metaphor and divergent-thinking ratings (−1.18 to .64 logits in their first study and about 0.9 in their second), although their ratings used other scales, rating formats and raters, so that logit spans are only indicatively comparable; severity differences of this size confound raw means whenever the design is incomplete [@primi2019; @hass2018]. [\[FILL IN: verify the primi2019 severity ranges (FI-17)\]]{.mark} For raters with many ratings, the differences in discrimination clearly exceeded the standard errors, for example between R09 ($a$ = 0.93, *SE* 0.15) and R06 (3.10, *SE* 0.45). The largest standard errors belonged to R18 for its thresholds and to R26, R19 and R27 for their discriminations, raters with 46–55 ratings; R26, R19 and R27 also had the widest information intervals. High discrimination, however, was not confined to imprecisely estimated raters (R06, R25 and R24 had 520, 138 and 190 ratings), so the spread in discrimination is not mainly estimation noise. The information shares are not a ranking of rater quality: they depend on the parameters as estimated, and for the raters with few ratings these are poorly determined. Read literally, one rating by the most informative rater (2.52) carries as much information as several ratings by the least informative (0.13), but the interval of the former runs from 0.11 to 6.75.

Because threshold spacing in the GRM is partly the same fact as discrimination, the raw response styles (@tbl-overview-rater-response-styles) carry the model-independent evidence on scale use, although they are not adjusted for which products each rater saw. Eight raters never used the top category, and R27 left a category inside the observed range unused. These differences are in line with reports of differing scale use and beliefs among CAT raters [@long2015] and with the rater effects described in rater-mediated assessment [@engelhard1994; @myford2003; @myford2004]. The contrast between raters who concentrated their ratings in the middle categories (e.g., R13) and raters who used the lowest category heavily (e.g., R06) corresponds to the central versus extreme responding discussed by @myszkowski2021; @primi2019 left such rater-by-scale interactions to future research. [\[FILL IN: verify the attributions to myszkowski2021 and primi2019 (FI-17)\]]{.mark} Expert status alone does not guarantee consensus [@hickey2001], and training and the selection of discerning raters are levers other than headcount [@storme2014; @ceh2022]. That the estimates of raters with few ratings are imprecise agrees with work showing that rater estimates in incomplete rating networks depend on the linking set [@wind2018; @wind2019] and that GRM parameter recovery requires adequate numbers of responses [@reise1990]. [\[FILL IN: verify the attributions to hickey2001, storme2014, ceh2022, wind2018, wind2019 and reise1990 (FI-17)\]]{.mark}

## RQ3: Constraints and consequences for scoring

The LR test rejected a shared category structure, but this constraint concerns M1 (rating-scale MFRM) only; M2 (partial-credit MFRM) already allows each rater their own category structure [@eckes2015]. Equal discrimination is the constraint shared by the whole Rasch family, and here, as for the shared category structure, the criteria disagreed: both constraints were rejected by the LR test and AIC but not by BIC. A possible explanation is that the BIC penalty grows with the number of parameters (GRM 158, M3 158, M2 135, M1 30), so that it weighs heavily against rater-specific parameters as the panel grows. The M3 discriminations spanned 0.305 to 2.221, a ratio of 7.277. The M1 fit values are consistent with the account that, in Rasch-family models, differences in discrimination surface only as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021]: R18 (M3 discrimination 0.305), R09 (0.306) and R17 (0.797), the three lowest discriminations in the ladder (@tbl-discrimination-m3), were the raters with values above 1 under M1, whereas R12 (2.169, the second-highest) had the lowest values under M1; the GRM discriminations give the same picture for R18, R09 and R12 (0.66, 0.93 and 2.72) but not for R17, whose GRM discrimination (1.81) is mid-range, so that for R17 the account holds under M3 only; the account is illustrative. Neither the unordered steps in M2 and M3 nor the ordered GRM thresholds count as evidence for either model family, because unordered steps indicate only that some category is never the most likely response [@andrich1978; @bond2020]. The GRM was preferred by AIC and SABIC, and a cumulative link is plausible for a unipolar creativity scale; @pellegrino2025 also retained a GRM for creativity ratings. The M1–M2 test compares models from different software, and this caveat stands.

Unweighted means treat raters as interchangeable, and when different raters rate different actions, the means are confounded with rater severity [@primi2019; @myszkowski2019]. In these data, products with the same single rating received GRM scores that spanned on average 1.229 and at most 1.430 (@fig-raw-mean-vs-theta). With one rating, a product's GRM score depends only on that rating and on the parameters of the rater who gave it, so this spread reflects differences between the raters as modelled, in both threshold location and discrimination; with two or more ratings, it also reflects the different combinations of ratings behind the same mean, which is part of the reason why .066 of the pairs were in reversed order with two ratings against .041 with one. As a range, it is set by the most extreme raters for each rating, some of whose parameters are imprecise (for example R18). Wherever actions are selected or ranked, for example to compile the most creative actions for training material, such reversals matter.

The choice among the models also shifted rankings: although all correlations with the GRM were .977 or higher, .206 of products changed quintile under M1 (rating-scale MFRM), with a mean percentile shift of .042, and .081 under M3 (GPCM), with a mean percentile shift of .016. A quintile change can also be a small move across a quintile boundary, so the two measures are best read together. Because the M1–GRM contrast combines the rater constraints with a change of link function, the two sources cannot be separated here. None of these comparisons shows that the GRM scores are more accurate than raw means or than the constrained models. The GRM adjusts for the modelled rater differences under its assumptions, but whether it predicts unseen ratings better was not examined, and it is not a validated criterion.

## Designing creativity-rating studies for nonverbal, time-pressured products

The implications are drawn from one rater pool, one 7-point scale and one product class. [\[FILL IN: rater-pool description to qualify this scope (FI-21)\]]{.mark} Five points follow. First, the number of ratings needed could not have been read off the existing evidence: the published figures come from other material, targets and objects, and the figure found here, four ratings for .80 in this rater pool, differs from them for reasons that these data cannot separate (domain, rater pool, scale, target and object). To our knowledge, this study supplies the first rating-design figures for football actions; rating-design evidence for nonverbal, time-pressured products therefore has to be collected, not assumed, since the number of raters needed remains an open question of the CAT [@cseh2019], each assessment procedure needs its own evidence [@vanhooijdonk2022], and most reviewed studies used fewer than 10 raters, about five on average [@long2022], a figure that does not rest on such evidence. Second, in these ratings of actions observed in competition, single ratings agreed weakly (Krippendorff's alpha .391) while raters differed strongly in severity, scale use and discrimination, so in such a pool, panels of three or four raters without a rater model would carry unquantified rater effects. Third, model-based scoring changed orderings enough to matter for selection. Fourth, a common calibration set of actions rated by all raters is distinct from rater training: training conflicts with the CAT rule of judgement without imposed criteria [@hennessey2011; @dollinger2005; @storme2014], a calibration set does not, and it stabilises the parameters of raters with few ratings only if these raters rate it and it is large enough. Fifth, about 50 ratings per rater (R17, R18, R19, R26 and R27) still left the parameters imprecise in these data, so no smaller number can be recommended from them. The recommendations are summarised in the box below.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Design recommendations for creativity ratings of actions in sport"}
1. Report the reliability of the scores actually used (empirical marginal reliability, product standard errors) and the agreement of single ratings, not only alpha or full-panel values (see @tbl-reliability-overview: .689 against .949 and .969; Krippendorff's alpha .391).
2. Plan the number of ratings per action with the precision of individual scores in mind: one or two ratings gave .522 and .699 here, and in this rater pool the smallest number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 was four (see @tbl-grm-reliability-by-n, @fig-grm-reliability-observed-vs-simulated and @tbl-grm-reliability-min-ratings).
3. Let all raters rate a sufficiently large common calibration set of actions, so that raters are linked and the parameters of raters with few ratings are estimated more precisely (the present design was connected; [\[FILL IN: confirm that no set of actions was rated by all raters; the largest fully crossed block comprised three raters and 261 actions (FI-4)\]]{.mark}).
4. Give each rater enough ratings for stable parameters; about 50 ratings per rater still left them imprecise here (see @tbl-grm-rater-parameters and @tbl-rater-overview).
5. Raters differed in severity, thresholds and discrimination, and raw means ordered actions partly differently from model-based scores (see @fig-m1-rater-severity and @tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm). Consider scoring actions with a model that adjusts for rater differences, under that model's assumptions, and report how far its ordering departs from the raw mean. This study does not show that model-based scores are more accurate.
6. Treat these figures as specific to this product class, rater pool and scale; rating-design figures from this or other material cannot be assumed to hold for other nonverbal, time-pressured products, rater pools or scales.
:::

## Limitations and future research

First, the rating design was incomplete, and the analysis assumes that the missing ratings are ignorable given the allocation of products to raters. [\[FILL IN: allocation procedure, including the second rater group (FI-4, FI-31)\]]{.mark} Ratings marked "action not recognised" were removed; if non-recognition depended on the action or the rater, the missingness is not ignorable. [\[FILL IN: non-recognition rate by rater (FI-22)\]]{.mark} The reliabilities by number of ratings are observational.

Second, the simulations rest on assumptions. In the projection, raters were drawn at random with equal probability, so the draws do not reproduce the raters' actual workloads; in the top-up simulation, the added raters were drawn with equal probability and without replacement from the panel raters who had not rated the product, so the added rater–product pairs do not follow the actual workloads either. In both, the parameters were treated as known, so the ranges omit parameter uncertainty; all ratings, including those of the kept rater–product pairs in the top-up simulation, were generated from the fitted GRM with $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$, so the simulations presuppose the model and the latent distribution and do not reuse the real ratings; the projection covers one to 10 ratings only; and no selected or workload-weighted rater sets were simulated. The number of ratings needed is therefore a figure for this rater pool under these assumptions.

Third, the fit evidence is limited: S-X² is conservative because most cells are imputed, C2 could not be computed, Q3 is negatively biased and its flag criterion has no reference distribution, and flags below 0.7 are expected with about two ratings per product. The absence of detected misfit is therefore not evidence of fit. The GRM had the lowest AIC and SABIC of the compared models, whereas BIC favoured M1; it is not a validated reference.

Fourth, the model comparison is not clear-cut. BIC disagreed with the LR test and AIC on both constraints, and the explanation offered above, the growth of the BIC penalty with the number of parameters, is a hypothesis. The M1–M2 test compares models from different software, with 105 degrees of freedom against the formula value of 115, reduced by the categories raters never used, including the internal gap of R27, and the M1–GRM contrast mixes rater constraints and link function.

Fifth, the parameters of raters with about 50 ratings are imprecise, and the parameter-draw intervals are conditional on valid draws. A normal latent distribution was assumed (standard normal in M3 and the GRM; estimated variance in M1 and M2), although the ratings concentrated at the low end of the scale. The response styles have no uncertainty, no confidence intervals exist for the agreement statistics, and the thresholds of R27 are not comparable with those of the other raters.

Sixth, the raters came from two groups, the second of which is not yet described, and whether they meet the CAT's requirement of domain familiarity is not established here. [\[FILL IN: characteristics of both rater groups (FI-1, FI-21, FI-31)\]]{.mark} Expertise was not analysed [@kaufman2009; @kaufman2013; @ceh2022; @hickey2001]. Seventh, the exclusion of raters with fewer than 15 ratings was a technical estimation criterion; it left the product scores nearly unchanged on average (*r* = .99994), with a largest change in one product score of 0.35026.

Eighth, the models had two facets and one dimension. They contain no facet for time or session, although rater tendencies can drift [@barth2021; @terai2026; @leckie2011; @myford2009] and workload affects agreement [@forthmann2017], and they do not test differential rater functioning [@wind2019a]; models such as the hierarchical rater model [@patz2002] or generalized many-facet models [@uto2020] could address this.

Several analyses were beyond the scope of this descriptive study and are left to future work: a test of rater severity on its own (a model without rater effects against the MFRM), the M1–M2 comparison within one software package, a held-out predictive check of model-based against raw-mean scores, projections that include parameter uncertainty and use selected or workload-weighted rater sets, a prospective design with a calibration set rated by all raters, rater covariates such as football expertise and panels of licensed coaches, other sports and other nonverbal, time-pressured products, and a G- and D-study of the same data. Until such evidence exists, the design implications above, several ratings per action, a calibration set rated by all raters and the reliability of the scores actually used, are what these data support.

# Conclusion

In these data, the reliability of the creativity scores actually obtained for football actions (.689) was far below the panel figures of .949 and .969. One or two ratings per action gave limited precision (.522 and .699), and in this rater pool the smallest number of ratings at which simulated reliability reached .80 was four. Raters differed in severity, scale use, discrimination and information, and the parameters of raters with about 50 ratings were imprecise. The shared category structure of M1 (rating-scale MFRM) and equal discrimination were rejected by the LR test and AIC but not by BIC, and both raw means and the constrained models ordered actions partly differently from the GRM. For nonverbal, time-pressured products such as football actions, rating-design figures from verbal or static material cannot be assumed to hold; they have to be collected for the product class and rater pool at hand. Studies of such products should report the reliability of the scores they use, plan several ratings per action, link raters through a common calibration set, and consider scoring with a model that adjusts for rater differences, reporting how far it departs from raw means. Whether such scores are more accurate remains to be examined.

## Simulated reliability by number of ratings {.unnumbered}

Two simulations from the fitted GRM complement the observed values. In the projection, products with $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$ were simulated; each received $k$ ratings ($k$ = 1 to 10) from $k$ distinct raters of the panel drawn at random, each rater equally likely to be drawn, so that the draws do not reproduce the raters' actual workloads. Ratings were generated from the fitted GRM and scored with its parameters, which were treated as known, in 50 replications of 2,000 simulated products per $k$ (seed 20260713). The table gives the empirical marginal reliability (mean and 95% range over replications) and the mean product-level reliability rel~post~. The top-up simulation (@tbl-grm-reliability-min-ratings in the main text) was built on the actual design and kept the actual assignment of raters to products, not the ratings. In the design labelled actual, each product kept exactly the raters who had rated it; in the design with at least four ratings per product, every product with fewer than four ratings was assigned additional raters, drawn at random with equal probability and without replacement from the panel raters who had not rated it, until it had four, and products with four or more ratings were unchanged. In each of 50 replications, every real product received $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$, all ratings for the kept and the added rater–product pairs were generated from the fitted GRM, and the products were scored by EAP with the parameters treated as known; the real ratings were not reused, and the actual-design row is a validation against the observed empirical reliability. Because the parameters are treated as known, the ranges reflect simulation variability only, not parameter uncertainty; the observed data remain primary. The last table places the observed mean rel~post~ of the actual products next to the simulated empirical marginal reliability; the two are different quantities.
